name: Lazarus Pharmaceuticals Splanchnic Triage Automaton
description:
The Splanchnic Triage Automaton is a palm-sized pneumatic chassis housing twelve articulated micro-manipulator arms, each tipped with a combination of ultrasonic scalpel, tissue-welding electrode, and biodegradable suture filament. Pressed against the abdomen and activated, the device uses subsurface acoustic imaging to map organ positions and identify perforations, bleeds, or torsions within a four-second diagnostic window. It then deploys its arms transdermally through guided puncture ports no wider than fourteen gauge, performing internal stabilization without requiring the patient to be opened. The procedure is described by those who have undergone it as feeling like a fist slowly unclenching inside the torso.

What distinguishes the Automaton from competing visceral repair tools is its onboard triage logic — a pre-trained decision model called CRISPIN — which prioritizes interventions by survivability probability rather than injury severity. CRISPIN will deliberately ignore a catastrophic but non-survivable wound to focus on a secondary bleed it calculates as recoverable. This has made the device controversial among surgeons who argue it removes human judgment from trauma triage, and revered among field medics who have watched it save lives that a human operator would have misspent effort on.

The device sees heavy use in GLMZ's outer-ring trauma corridors, where licensed paramedics carry it as a last-resort stabilizer before transport. It is also a fixture in the kits of corporate extraction teams, who value its ability to keep a compromised asset alive long enough to reach a proper surgical facility. Unlicensed copies, stripped of CRISPIN's ethical limiters, circulate in black-market medical stalls under the name 'The Undertaker's Hands' — a designation that refers, depending on who you ask, to the device's lifesaving reach or to what happens when it is used without proper calibration.
tactical_use: Deployed in the field when abdominal trauma is suspected and surgical facilities are unavailable or hours away. The medic presses the chassis flush against the patient's abdomen, initiates the acoustic scan, and allows CRISPIN to select its intervention targets. The operator can override CRISPIN's priority queue manually, though Lazarus Pharmaceuticals formally disclaims liability when this occurs. The device is not a substitute for surgery — it is a bridge, buying hours rather than providing resolution. In extraction scenarios, it is used in conjunction with sedation to keep a patient immobile during deployment, as involuntary movement during transdermal arm extension can cause secondary laceration.
cultural_context: The Splanchnic Triage Automaton occupies an uncomfortable space in GLMZ's medical culture. Licensed surgeons view it with institutional suspicion — the CRISPIN logic's willingness to make survivability calls is seen as an encroachment on clinical authority, and several high-profile cases where CRISPIN deprioritized a wound that a human surgeon would have caught have fed ongoing litigation. Among street medics and outer-ring paramedics, however, it is regarded as close to sacred. The black-market variant, 'The Undertaker's Hands,' carries a more ambivalent reputation — equally capable of saving a ganger's life and of being used to perform coerced internal procedures on unwilling patients when its ethical limiters are removed.
story_hooks: A black-market Undertaker's Hands unit surfaces with CRISPIN replaced by a custom logic model that seems to be making decisions no standard triage algorithm should be capable of — as if it is learning patient histories it has no access to.

A corporate extraction medic used the Automaton on a client who survived — but CRISPIN's logs, subpoenaed in a wrongful death suit against a third party, contain acoustic imaging data that proves the client was somewhere they claimed not to be.

A street medic discovers her licensed unit has been remotely updated with a new CRISPIN build that behaves differently than the old one — deprioritizing injuries that match a specific demographic profile in ways she cannot explain.

An outer-ring clinic is offering Automaton procedures at a fraction of standard cost. The patients are surviving, but several have reported finding small objects — unfamiliar and unaccounted for — lodged in their abdominal cavities post-procedure.

physical_description.visual_profile: A sleek, ovoid chassis roughly the size of a deck of cards, tapered at one end with a soft-touch adhesion surface designed to conform to skin topography. When collapsed, it resembles a high-end medical injector or compact diagnostic scanner. The micro-manipulator arms are housed internally and invisible until deployment, giving the device an almost innocent, clinical appearance.
physical_description.dimensions: 11cm × 7cm × 4cm (collapsed); expands to approximately 15cm when arms are partially extended during operation
physical_description.weight_description: 340g with full suture load — handheld, fits easily in a parammedic's cargo pocket or extraction kit. Light enough for prolonged field carry but substantial enough to feel engineered and robust.
physical_description.primary_material: Titanium-reinforced polymer chassis with medical-grade silicone contact surface; pneumatic manifold housing brushed stainless steel
physical_description.finish: Satin anodized titanium with matte medical-white polymer sections; the adhesion surface is soft-touch silicone with faint textured grip zones. Minimal reflectivity to reduce surgical glare.
physical_description.color_scheme: Clinical white and gunmetal gray dominant; accent striping in cool cyan (diagnostic indicators) and amber-orange (warning/power states). The suture cartridge window reveals spools of translucent biodegradable filament.
physical_description.interface_elements: Recessed activation button (pressure-sensitive), micro LED status matrix (4-dot diagnostic readout), cartridge ejection lever, wireless coupling node (for CRISPIN telemetry), and a small monochrome OLED display (1.2 inches) showing battery/suture load and procedure countdown. Magnetic docking contacts for charging cradle.
distinctive_features: Subsurface acoustic imaging lens (faint honeycomb pattern visible on ventral surface)
Twelve retractable puncture-port guidance sheaths with visible 14-gauge tips when partially deployed
Pulsing cyan LED beneath the chassis indicating active CRISPIN diagnostic mode
Suture cartridge window showing colorful filament spools in graduated tension holders
Distinctive soft-touch adhesion pad with subtle radiating grip texture — feels almost biological
physical_description.manufacturer_markings: Lazarus Medical Devices logo (stylized serpent entwined around a caduceus) stamped in micro-print on dorsal surface. Regulatory stamps: GLMZ Medical Authority certification, CRISPIN v4.1 model designation, batch number, and a small Φ price code. Serial number laser-etched on battery housing.
physical_description.condition_typical: In field use, often appears dust-covered or lightly bloodstained on the adhesion surface; paramedics keep them in sterile polymer cases between deployments. The OLED display frequently shows dim battery warnings mid-shift. Well-used units show micro-scratches on the diagnostic lens and slight discoloration of the silicone pad from repeated skin contact.
